Self-Examination
SELF-eg-zam-ih-NAY-shun
n.
From Latin examinare, to weigh, test, try; rendering the Greek peirazō and dokimazō in Paul's "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves" (2 Cor 13:5).

Biblical Definition

Self-Examination is the duty whereby a Christian honestly tries his own heart, faith, and life before God, to discern whether he be truly in the faith and to detect and mortify his besetting sins. Paul commands it directly: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?" (2 Cor 13:5). The verbs are peirazō and dokimazō, to test and to prove as metal is assayed for its genuineness. A particular and solemn occasion of this duty is the approach to the Lord's table: "But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup" (1 Cor 11:28), lest he eat and drink unworthily and bring judgment on himself. The Puritans were masters of this exercise, urging the saints to spread their hearts open before the all-seeing God, to compare their state with the marks of grace the word lays down—love of the brethren, hatred of sin, delight in God's law, the keeping of His commandments—and so to make their calling and election sure. Self-examination has two great uses: it confirms the assurance of the sincere, who upon trial find the evidences of grace; and it disturbs the false peace of the hypocrite and the formalist, who upon trial find nothing of Christ within. Yet it must be carefully distinguished from a morbid, anxious introspection that turns the soul perpetually inward upon itself, breeds doubt and despair, and never lifts the eye to Christ. Healthy self-examination always issues in fresh recourse to the Savior—searching the heart that one may flee anew to the blood that cleanseth, not that one may rest in the search. This dictionary confesses self-examination as a necessary and wholesome duty of the Christian, commanded in the word, practised before the Supper, aimed at the trial of one's faith and the mortification of sin, and ever ending not in self but in Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines EXAMINATION as the act of examining; a careful search or inquiry with a view to discover truth. Self-Examination is the believer's honest trying of his own heart, faith, and life before God (2 Cor 13:5).

expand to see more

EXAMINATION, n. — The act of examining; a careful search or inquiry with a view to discover truth; the act of viewing or considering; inquiry into facts or principles by interrogatories.

SELF-EXAMINATION, n. — An examination into one's own state, conduct, and motives, particularly in regard to religious feelings and duties.

"Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves" (2 Cor 13:5).

It requires the honest trial of one's faith by the marks of grace in the word, especially before the Lord's Supper; it forbids the morbid introspection that never looks to Christ.

It confirms the assurance of the sincere and disturbs the false peace of the hypocrite—ever ending not in self, but in Christ.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 13:5 — "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?"

1 Corinthians 11:28 — "But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup."

Psalms 139:23-24 — "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting."

Lamentations 3:40 — "Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Self-Examination is corrupted on one side by the neglect that lets men live in false peace untried, and on the other by a morbid, anxious introspection that turns the soul perpetually inward and never flees to Christ.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruptions of this duty are the old ones. The first is simple neglect—the unexamined profession that takes its own salvation for granted, never tries itself by the marks of grace, and so rests in a false peace that the day of judgment will shatter. Against this Paul commands, "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith" (2 Cor 13:5), and warns that a man may approach the Lord's table unworthily, eating and drinking judgment to himself, for want of self-trial (1 Cor 11:28-29). The positive principle to recover is the wholesome Puritan practice of trying one's heart honestly before the all-seeing God—"Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Ps 139:23)—comparing one's state with the evidences of true grace the word describes, that the calling and election may be made sure.

The opposite corruption is morbid introspection—an endless, anxious turning of the eye inward that breeds scrupulosity, doubt, and despair, dissecting every motive until the soul is paralyzed and Christ is lost from view. This is not the self-examination Scripture commands but a snare of the enemy, who, if he cannot keep a man careless, will make him morbidly self-occupied. The recovery is to mark the proper end of the duty: self-examination is never an end in itself and never terminates upon the self. Its purpose is to drive the soul afresh to Christ—to find sin that one may mortify it, to find grace that one may bless God for it, and in either case to flee anew to the Savior. Healthy trial of the heart always ends with the eye lifted off self and fixed upon the blood that cleanseth from all sin.

Hebrew Roots

The duty rests on Paul's heautous peirazete... dokimazete (2 Cor 13:5), the trying and proving of one's own self in the faith, and the self-examination before the Supper (1 Cor 11:28).

expand to see more

Greek peirazō (G3985) — to test, try, prove; "examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith" (2 Cor 13:5).

Greek dokimazō (G1381) — to prove, assay as metal; "prove your own selves," testing for genuineness.

Hebrew chaqar (H2713) — to search out, examine; "search me, O God, and know my heart" (Ps 139:23).

Hebrew chaphas (H2664) — to search diligently; "let us search and try our ways" (Lam 3:40).

The trial is the honest weighing of heart and life by the word, ever ending not in self but in Christ.

Usage

"Before coming to the Lord's table, the godly man practised Self-Examination, trying his heart honestly before God."

"Paul's command, "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith," binds every professor to Self-Examination."

"True Self-Examination is no morbid introspection; it tries the heart only to drive the soul afresh to Christ."
